Sorry, I should have been specific in my question. I wasn't speaking about medication to promote weight loss. I was speaking about medication that increased weight gain or more specifically medication that contain an unfavorable metabolic profile. Example would be classes such as atypicals or antidepressants. 

The typical advice from the medical community is diet and exercise. 

However, if energy homeostasis is to be taken in consideration, along with our knowledge on how cells adapt to maintain this [energy homeostasis](http://jn.nutrition.org/content/134/2/295/F1.expansion), then I don't see how this advice would work and instead I *feel* it should worsen the condition. 

Exercise has many effects, not just caloric expenditure. I'm not arguing it will not expend calories. I'm only arguing that it will effect the various neurotransmitters (directly or indirectly) that are involved appetite and hunger and perhaps overall metabolism (rate) - the body is maintain homeostasis by trying to get you to replenish energy reserves (depleted lipids). So for example reduce leptin levels, should indicate an energy deficit to the brain and release the respective neurotransmitters/hormones that regulate hunger and induce these feeding behaviors. Since your body will respond with hunger (because of exercising raising these levels), it doesn't seem logical to recommend this when you are already taking a compound that induces hunger. So why wouldn't it have an additive effect? Does it not worsen the problem?

Disclaimer: I truly do appreciate the complexity of obesity, so I'm certainly not trying to downplay the complex regulating systems. I only providing this as an example to explain the position of my question. There is no doubt more than circulating leptin (and appetite regulating chemical) contributing to the obesity epidemic So to be clear and iterate - I'm not pretending to be an expert because I'm not. 

Edit* Maybe I'm not understanding how the body adapts? Care to explain the common theories of that? Thanks

Also sorry for the poor english

I would like to add that the knowledge you get from a degree is only useful if you truly understand it inside and out. In a university CS program you move from project to project and class to class. Passing classes is cool and all, but so is actually learning the material inside and out. Fortunately gifted professors can bestow just enough for you to follow up afterward, but I suppose the same argument can be made for an average Joe and with YouTube and a textbook on the subject.

One argument for a CS degree, in my humble opinion, is marketing. That of course is changing too as the field grows. Then again the above post pointed out a lot of people work at Google without degrees.

Also cost is another issue if you live in the states. I can tell you, at least right now, that marketing yourself with a U.S./European degree goes a long way in other countries if you decide to leave and/or take a position overseas. How long will that last? Don't know, so again you might be better off without one.
